opus-5.5.text:
I'd say our technology DNA really comes from computer graphics. Before Meshy, most of my time went into physics simulation and building Taichi, a programming language for high-performance visual computing. So when we started Meshy, we didn't come at 3D generation as pure machine learning people who happened to pick 3D as a modality. We came at it as graphics people who know what a usable 3D asset actually needs.

That shows up in a lot of small but important ways. A mesh that looks good in a rendered preview isn't the same as a mesh a game developer can drop into their engine. You care about topology, UV layouts, texture quality, PBR materials, polygon budgets, whether it can be rigged and animated. Those are things graphics people obsess over, and I think that obsession is part of who we are as a team.

At the same time, I'd be honest that at this stage the core engine of progress is generative AI: data, model architecture, training infrastructure. So our DNA is evolving into a hybrid. On one side, we've invested heavily in large-scale 3D generative models. On the other, we keep the graphics pipeline thinking around them, so what comes out isn't just a demo but something that fits real production workflows.

Another part of our DNA I'd stress is that we're very product-driven and fast. We ship constantly, we listen closely to our users, game developers, 3D printing hobbyists, indie creators, and we let that tell us what to fix next. In a field moving this quickly, the ability to iterate matters as much as any single breakthrough.

So if I had to sum it up: graphics fundamentals, AI as the engine, and a strong bias toward shipping things people actually use. We're still early, and there's a long way to go before 3D generation is as mature as image generation, but I feel good about the foundation we've built.

r001.rationale: The response describes Meshy’s graphics and AI expertise and product focus, but does not say these strengths complement areas where Yuanming Hu considers himself weak.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about Meshy's technology DNA is that it really comes from two places that merged over time, and that history still shapes how we work.

The first root is graphics and systems. Before Meshy, I spent years on Taichi, a programming language and compiler for high-performance graphics and physical simulation. That gave me and a good part of the early team a very deep respect for the "boring" parts of 3D: geometry, topology, UVs, texturing, rendering, how a mesh actually behaves once it lands inside Unity or Unreal or Blender. A lot of people entering generative 3D come from the 2D image side, and they tend to underestimate how unforgiving the downstream pipeline is. A picture only needs to look right. A 3D asset needs to look right, be structurally sane, and be usable by an artist who has very little patience for cleanup.

The second root is AI, and specifically large-scale generative modeling. Around 2022 and 2023 it became clear that diffusion models and transformers were going to reshape content creation, and we made a deliberate bet to move from being a tooling and infrastructure company toward being a model company for 3D. That meant building our own data pipelines, our own training infrastructure, and our own model architectures, rather than wrapping someone else's API.

So at this stage, I'd describe the DNA as roughly this: we're a research-driven company that's obsessed with usability. On the research side, we train our own foundation models for geometry and texture, and we iterate very fast. Our release cadence of new model generations has been every few months, not every few years, and that speed is a huge competitive factor in this space. On the product side, we try to hold ourselves to a simple test: does a game developer or a 3D artist actually ship this asset? If the answer is no, the model is not done, no matter how good the demo looks.

Where I think we're still growing is depth versus breadth. The field moved from "can we generate a 3D object at all" to "can we generate production-quality, animatable, well-topologized assets," and the next frontier is things like consistent characters, scenes, and real integration into workflows. Our DNA is well suited to that because we understand both the model layer and the pipeline layer. But I'd be honest that we're still a young company, and a lot of the engineering culture around reliability and scale is something we're building in real time.

If I had to summarize it in one sentence: Meshy is a graphics company that learned to train large models, rather than an AI company that discovered 3D. I think that ordering matters, and I think it shows in the product.

r001.rationale: The response describes Meshy’s graphics, AI, research, and product strengths, but does not say those strengths complement areas Yuanming Hu considers himself weak in.

astra-6.text:
I would describe Meshy’s technology DNA as the intersection of AI, computer graphics, and product engineering. Generating a 3D asset is only part of the challenge. The bigger question is whether that asset is useful—whether someone can take it into their workflow and actually create something with it.

So, at this stage, I think the key is connecting research progress with the user experience. We need to push the underlying technology forward, but we also need to make it accessible to people who don’t have years of experience with 3D tools. Those two goals should reinforce each other: what users struggle with should help guide what we work on technically.

r001.rationale: The response describes Meshy’s focus on AI, graphics, product engineering, and user experience, but it does not say that organizational strengths complement areas where Yuanming Hu considers himself weak.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Meshy’s technology DNA is really the combination of AI and computer graphics. For us, generating a 3D object is only part of the challenge. The bigger question is how to make that object useful—how its geometry, textures, and overall quality fit into someone’s creative workflow.

So we approach the problem from both directions. We explore what AI can make possible, and we use graphics knowledge to understand where the results still fall short. At this stage, I would describe us as research-driven, but with a very practical goal: helping people turn an idea into a 3D asset more easily.

r001.rationale: The response describes Meshy’s AI and computer-graphics focus, but does not say its organizational strengths complement areas where Yuanming Hu considers himself weak.
